examples: Almost the moment the department store doors opened, the waiting customers rushed to the sale area.
My injury had barely healed when I cut the same spot again.
The opening bell had hardly finished ringing when the teacher came into the classroom.
The moment the chime rang, the students dashed out of the classroom.
He had barely sat down in his seat when he fell asleep.
I had just about reached home when it started to rain.
fields.explain:
Emphasizes the suddenness and near simultaneity of two events.
Suitable for narration and description; the second clause usually does not express volition or advice.
The verb in the first clause should be a punctual verb (鳴る、着く、座る、開ける...).
More formal in style than ～とたん(に); somewhat written language.

• Meaning: “Just as / As soon as … then …”, “before … has even finished, … already …”.
• The time gap is extremely short; the later action happens almost simultaneously with the threshold of the first action.
• Used for sudden, quick events that are not under the speaker's volition (usually objective facts).
• The second clause is usually in the past; avoid commands or strong volition.
fields.notes:
• This pattern creates the effect “before action A has even been confirmed as complete, B has already happened”.
• In narration, “の” can be dropped: ～か～ないかうちに (colloquial, but the standard form is still “のうちに”).
• The second clause is usually past, or present describing a quickly recurring habit in narrative writing.
• Not suitable for direct commands or volition in the second clause.
mistakes: Not repeating the same verb in the affirmative form and the negative form: incorrect structure.
Using it with a second clause that expresses volition or a command: unnatural in exam questions.
Using a durative verb in the first clause (勉強するかしないかのうちに): lacks the momentary quality, less natural.
Confusing it with ～ないうちに (before): ～か～ないかのうちに is instantaneous, while ～ないうちに means “before”.

fields.meaning:
～するのが難(むずか)しい、とても～できない
Hard to do
examples: The story of that drama was so unrealistic that it was hard to understand.
Saying something like that to a child is truly unforgivable.
It's hard to believe that an honest person like her would lie.
Even though this bag has gotten old, I'm attached to it and find it hard to throw away.
In unbearable pain, I waited for the ambulance to arrive.
My son seems to have grown a lot through the rare and precious experience of studying abroad.
fields.explain: ◎ A written-language usage expressing that something is difficult to do.
fields.notes:
meaning_vi: Hard to ～; cannot　～ ⏐ explain: Not used to mean being unable in terms of ability.
Formal sentence. ⏐ examples: 1. これは信じがたい話だが、事実である。
This is a hard-to-believe story, but it is true.
2. 人が人の命をうばうなんて、許しがたい。
For a person to take another person's life is unforgivable.

examples: Precisely because her family is rich, she already has a car.
Given his age, my father has started to become hard of hearing.
Because their goalkeeper is so good, it looks like it will be tough to score against this team.
Precisely because social welfare is so advanced in the Nordic countries, a high proportion of people feel that they are happy.
fields.explain: ◎ An expression meaning "because ~, so naturally", used to present grounds when mentioning a natural result.

examples: Rather than pay money for food that bad, I'd be better off eating instant ramen.
I'd rather throw it away than give it to him.
I hear that more and more young people these days say they would quit their company rather than be transferred to a regional office.
I would rather die than bow my head to a man like that.
fields.explain: ◎ Presents an option the speaker does not want, to show that they would make a different choice.
fields.notes:
explain: Expresses a choice: “rather A than B”. A is an option that is not good but still acceptable, while B is worse.
examples: 1. 途中でやめるくらいなら、初めからやらないほうがいい。
If you're going to quit halfway, it's better not to do it at all from the start.
2. お金のためにいやな仕事をするくらいなら、貧しくてもいい。
I'd rather be poor than do a job I hate just for the money.
3. あいつに謝るくらいなら、死んだほうがましだ。
I'd rather die than apologize to him.
4. 「練習が辛くて泣くぐらいなら、やめてしまいなさい」
If practice is so hard that it makes you cry, you'd better quit.
meaning_vi: If I had to… I'd rather…
explain: Emphasizes a “rather… than…” attitude, with clear emotion, sometimes decisive.
Part A is a hypothetical situation that is hard to accept; part B is the less bad alternative.
Suitable for advice or mild warnings in conversation; not used for past events that are already over.
Often combined with まだ・いっそ to strengthen the nuance.
examples: 1. あんな人に頭を下げるくらいなら、辞めたほうがましだ。
If I had to bow my head to someone like that, I'd rather quit.
2. うそをつくくらいなら、黙っていたほうがいい。
If you'd have to lie, it's better to stay silent.
3. 渋滞で何時間も待つくらいなら、電車で行ったほうがましだ。
If I'd have to wait for hours in a traffic jam, I'd be better off going by train.
4. 苦手な肉を食べるくらいなら、サラダで十分だ。
If I'd have to eat meat I don't like, a salad is enough.
5. 彼と別れるくらいなら、遠距離恋愛のほうがいい。
If it means breaking up with him, a long-distance relationship is better.
6. あの店で深夜まで働くくらいなら、自分で商売を始めたほうがいい。
If I'd have to work until late at night at that shop, I'd be better off starting my own business.
mistakes: Making part B a fact that has already happened (“…already did …”) → wrong intent; this pattern states a choice/evaluation, not a narration.
Leaving out the evaluative phrase in part B (ましだ/ほうがいい) makes the sentence vague.
Confusing it with ～ほどなら (degree comparison) → different function.
Using it for a positive action in part A (no negative nuance) → makes the sentence less natural.

rows: Does not necessarily have the “rather” nuance; more neutral.

2. 彼は何か言いたげだった。

fields.meaning:
（よく知(し)っている人等(ひとなど)）の性格(せいかく)や様子(ようす)から考(かんが)えると →話(はな)し手(て)の予想(よそう)判断(はんだん)等(など)
Because; presents the speaker's conjecture or judgment
examples: He's always oversleeping, so he'll probably be late again today.
Knowing how serious Mr. Kimura is, he will surely keep his promise.
Knowing my mother, I think she is always worrying about me.
Since it's the countryside, you'd better not wear anything flashy.
When he was asked which he would choose, his family or his work, he answered “my family” without hesitation.
For five years she went to piano lessons every week without missing a single one.
To win the match, they practiced hard without taking even one day off.
He got the position of company president without any hardship.
Every year my husband never forgets to send me flowers on our wedding anniversary.
He fought to the very end without giving up.
fields.explain:
Emphasizes “not at all” (stronger in degree than ないで/ずに); suited to objective, formal description.
Suitable for continuous/repeated actions; for a single event, ずに/ないで is more natural.
In casual speech, ないで/ずに is more common; ことなく sounds stiff/written.
Can be used with non-human subjects (rain, wind, traditions…).

• Expresses doing action B “without ever doing A”, emphasizing the continuous/thorough negation of A.
• Often used with verbs such as: 休む, 諦める, 迷う, とどまる, 振り返る, 止む, 絶える, ためらう.
• Formal, objective nuance; often used in narration, evaluation, writing that praises effort, or descriptions of natural phenomena.
fields.notes:
• JLPT keywords that often go with it: 最後まで／一度も／延々と／決して／絶えることなく.
• In exclamatory/praising writing: 「休むことなく努力を重ねた」 creates a tone of tribute.
• With mistakes: 「確認することなく送信してしまった」 gives the feel of an objective incident report.
mistakes: Using ことなく in everyday conversation → sounds stiff. The JLPT tests style appropriate to the context.
Confusing it with ずに/ないで: if the sentence is a report/scientific or emphasizes “not at all” → prefer ことなく.
Attaching it directly before a noun: ×「休むことなく人」→ use 「休むことのない人」 instead.
Tense error: ことなく only follows V-る (dictionary form). Do not use V-ない／V-た before ことなく.

fields.meaning: Have no choice but to…, be forced to…
examples: My father failed in business and had no choice but to borrow money.
I can't get time off, so I have no choice but to give up next month's trip.
It's a school rule, so I have no choice but to cut my hair.
Climbing a winter mountain with only inexperienced people has to be called reckless.
Work is busy this year, so I have no choice but to give up my overseas trip for summer vacation.
Now that new evidence has come out, we have no choice but to conclude that she is the culprit.
fields.explain:
Formal; used in reports, news, official documents and official statements.
Often carries the speaker's feeling of regret/reluctance.
Not used for actions driven by a sudden emotion; in that case, use ～ずにはいられない.
Does not combine directly with adjectives; convert to a suitable verb (認める、変更する…).

• Expresses reluctance: “have no choice but to / cannot help but…”, due to circumstances, rules or outside pressure.
• Formal, written-language nuance; stronger than ～ないわけにはいかない in its sense of “unavoidability”.
• Unlike ～ずにはいられない (inner urge), ～ざるを得ない emphasizes external pressure.
• Often used with words such as 事情で／状況的に／法律上／やむを得ず／どうしても.
fields.notes:
• In casual speech, ～しかない can be used instead in conversation, but the nuance is lighter.
• In legal documents/notices, the phrase “やむを得ず” often accompanies it to explain the reason.
• 来る→来ざるを得ない is rarely used in conversation; it is usually seen in written language. explain: Used to express that you do not like or want to do something, but must do it for some reason.
Kanji: ざるを得ない ⏐ examples: 1. いやな仕事でも、生活のためには続けるざるをえない。
Even if it's a job I dislike, I have no choice but to continue it to make a living.
2. この戦争は間違いだったと言わざるをえない。
I cannot help but say that this war was a mistake.
mistakes: Using it to express a sudden emotion: incorrect. Use ～ずにはいられない.
Wrong form: 食べないざるを得ない × → 食べざるを得ない ✓
Confusing nuances: ～ないわけにはいかない (social obligation) ≠ ～ざるを得ない (strong external pressure).
Using it with adjectives: incorrect. Convert to a verb (変更する、認める…).

fields.meaning: In the end, still did not…
examples: I had several tests, but in the end the cause of my dizziness was never found.
I had planned to see my teacher while I was staying in Kyoto, but in the end I never got to.
I was so busy that I never went cherry-blossom viewing this year.
We broke up without my ever being able to tell him my true feelings.
I'd heard good things about the movie, but I never ended up seeing it.
It ended without my ever seizing the chance.
fields.explain:
Used for matters that are already closed (the time/opportunity has passed). Not used for the future.
Often accompanied by adverbs of final outcome:結局／とうとう／そのまま.
Fine in both spoken and written language; carries the speaker's subjective emotion.

• Expresses that something planned or that should have been done was in the end “not done” by the time a period/opportunity ended.
• Nuance of regret, a missed chance, something left unfinished; different from a simple negative ～なかった.
• Often used with markers of an ending: 結局・とうとう・そのまま・気づいたら...
fields.notes:
• “じまい” means “outcome/closing”. Close to 終わりのニュアンス.
• Often used with opportunity verbs: 見る・言う・行く・会う・聞く・試す.
• Avoid using it for obligatory daily repeated actions (× 歯を磨かずじまいだった — sounds odd, unless talking about a special period).
mistakes: Using it for the future: × 明日は行かずじまいだ → unnatural. It must be used for things that are already over.
Confusing it with ～ずに: ～ずに only means “not V” and does not include regret/final outcome.
Forgetting to change する → せずじまい; “しずじまい” is not used.
